passages.title: New Agriculture in Oregon, US
passages.subtitle: How innovative drip irrigation is transforming onion farming in the American West

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Onion growers in eastern Oregon are adopting a system that saves water and keeps topsoil in place, while producing the highest quality 'super colossal' onions. County agents and researchers with Oregon State University (OSU) Extension Service have been working with growers to explore ways to reduce water use and improve irrigation efficiency. In the Malheur River Basin of eastern Oregon, growers have worked with researchers to develop a drip irrigation system for onions that reduces water use by up to 50 percent, reduces erosion and minimizes the runoff of pesticides and fertilizers into streams and groundwater.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The project is a model for how researchers and farmers can work together to address environmental concerns while maintaining agricultural productivity. The Malheur River Basin produces about a third of the nation's storage onions, but traditional furrow irrigation was washing valuable topsoil and chemicals into waterways. Researchers at OSU's Malheur Experiment Station in Ontario, Oregon, began experimenting with buried drip irrigation tape in the early 1990s. In furrow-irrigated fields, water flows down trenches between rows of crops. In drip-irrigated fields, perforated plastic tubes buried beneath the crop rows deliver water and nutrients directly to plant roots in precise amounts.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The results have been dramatic. In addition to cutting water use by up to half, drip irrigation has increased crop yields and improved onion size and quality. Drip irrigation keeps the soil moisture consistent, preventing the fluctuations that cause onions to split or develop multiple centers. It also prevents the spread of soil-borne diseases by keeping the onion foliage dry. Because fertilizer and pesticides are delivered directly through the drip tubes, less chemical is needed and far less runs off into nearby streams.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Growers were initially hesitant to adopt the system because of the high upfront costs—about $1,000 to $1,500 per acre to install the drip tape, filters, pumps and tubing. However, many growers have found that the system pays for itself within three to five years through water savings, reduced chemical costs, and higher yields of premium-grade onions. Furthermore, state and federal cost-share programs have helped offset the initial capital expenditure.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The success of drip irrigation in onions has led researchers and farmers to test the system on other crops in the region, including sugar beets, potatoes and alfalfa. Research horticulturist Clint Shock and his colleagues at the Malheur Experiment Station continue to refine the technology, developing automated sensors and computer controls that adjust irrigation schedules based on soil moisture and weather conditions. Their work has attracted interest from agricultural researchers and farmers worldwide who face similar water shortages.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Despite these successes, challenges remain. Disposal of the plastic drip tape after each growing season poses an environmental problem, prompting researchers to seek recyclable or biodegradable alternatives. In addition, rodents and insects can chew holes in the buried tape, causing leaks that require vigilant monitoring and repair. Nevertheless, growers who have made the transition say the benefits far outweigh the challenges.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The Malheur Basin project illustrates how sustainable agricultural practices can emerge through collaborative research, economic incentives, and grower leadership. By demonstrating that environmental stewardship and economic viability can go hand in hand, eastern Oregon's onion growers are charting a course for the future of irrigated agriculture in the arid American West.

passages.title: Intelligence and Giftedness
passages.subtitle: The origins of psychometrics and the modern understanding of cognitive potential

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In 1904 the French minister of education, facing limited resources for schooling, sought a way to separate the unable from the merely lazy. Alfred Binet got the job of devising selection principles and his brilliant solution put a stamp on the study of intelligence and was the forerunner of modern psychometrics. Together with Théodore Simon, Binet created the first practical intelligence scale to identify children who needed special educational assistance.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Binet's test was quickly translated, revised, and widely embraced in the United States. Lewis Terman of Stanford University adapted the test into the Stanford-Binet Intelligence Scale and popularized the concept of the Intelligence Quotient (IQ), calculated by dividing mental age by chronological age and multiplying by 100. During World War I, the US Army developed group intelligence tests—the Army Alpha and Beta tests—to classify more than a million recruits, cementing standardized testing in American society.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: However, Binet himself warned against misinterpreting his scale. He never intended IQ to measure fixed, innate intelligence; rather, he designed it as a diagnostic tool to pinpoint areas where children could benefit from remedial education. Binet believed intelligence was multifaceted and modifiable, a view echoed by many modern educational psychologists who caution against treating a single test score as an immutable verdict on human potential.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Psychologists have long debated what intelligence actually consists of. Charles Spearman proposed the concept of a general intelligence factor, or 'g', which underlies all cognitive abilities. In contrast, researchers like Howard Gardner have argued for multiple intelligences, proposing that humans possess distinct forms of intellect ranging from linguistic and logical-mathematical to musical, spatial, bodily-kinesthetic, and interpersonal abilities.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The study of giftedness has similarly evolved. Early researchers defined gifted children solely in terms of high IQ scores, usually above 130. Today, giftedness is recognized as encompassing creative thinking, task commitment, leadership, and artistic talent. Programs for gifted students increasingly employ multidimensional assessments rather than relying exclusively on standardized test results.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Environmental factors play a crucial role in the development of intelligence and giftedness. Access to stimulating educational resources, supportive family environments, and opportunities for deliberate practice strongly influence whether innate potential translates into exceptional achievement. Research demonstrates that high ability without nurture often languishes, while average initial ability paired with rich environmental support can lead to extraordinary accomplishments.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Contemporary psychometrics continues to wrestle with questions of cultural fairness, validity, and the predictive power of standardized tests. While intelligence tests remain widely used in clinical diagnostics, education, and employment selection, psychologists emphasize that they measure only a slice of human cognitive capacity, and must be interpreted with caution alongside broader measures of creativity, emotional intelligence, and perseverance.

passages.title: Paper or Computer?
passages.subtitle: The cognitive science of physical documents versus digital screens in modern offices

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Computer technology was supposed to replace paper. But that hasn't happened. Every country in the Western world uses more paper today, on a per-capita basis, than it did ten years ago. The consumption of uncoated free-sheet paper, for instance—the most common kind of office paper—rose almost fifteen percent in the United States between 1995 and 2000. This is not just a stubborn attachment to obsolete habits; cognitive psychologists and ergonomics experts argue that paper persists for very good reasons.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: When it comes to reading and thinking, paper has unique physical properties, or 'affordances', that digital screens struggle to match. Paper is tangible: we can hold it, feel its weight, flip through pages rapidly, and spread multiple documents across a desk. Paper enables spatial navigation that gives readers a continuous sense of where they are in a text, supporting comprehension and long-term memory in ways that scrolling across a screen often disrupts.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Paper is also exceptionally tailorable. We can easily annotate it, highlight passages, and scribble margin notes as we read, without altering the underlying text or navigating complicated menus. In collaborative settings, printed documents provide a shared physical artifact that group members can view, point to, and discuss simultaneously without fighting over a keyboard or mouse.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Studies of office workers reveal that the apparent mess of papers on desks often reflects sophisticated cognitive management. Cognitive psychologist Alison Kidd observed that knowledge workers frequently keep documents in active piles rather than filing them away in cabinets. These piles serve as physical reminders and contextual cues, allowing workers to track multiple ongoing projects without losing their train of thought.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Digital documents, of course, offer distinct advantages. They can be searched instantly, stored without taking up physical space, edited effortlessly, and transmitted across the globe in seconds. Yet attempts to impose entirely paperless offices frequently encounter resistance because they ignore the complementary roles of digital tools and physical paper.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Rather than viewing paper and computers as adversaries in a winner-take-all battle, forward-thinking organizations recognize that each medium has strengths suited to different cognitive tasks. Paper excels for deep reading, reflection, drafting, and interpersonal collaboration, while digital media excel for archiving, data analysis, and rapid communication. The modern office flourishes when both technologies work together harmoniously.
